title: File systems, protection, virtual machines and contemporary systems
subtitle: How bytes become named files, how access is controlled, and how one machine pretends to be many. The chapter finishes the operating system story: storage organisation, protection, security, virtualisation and a tour of real systems.

sections.title: The file abstraction
sections.body:
Memory is volatile and small; processes need somewhere permanent to keep programs and data. The OS provides it as the file: a named, persistent collection of bytes, however the disk actually stores them. A file has a name, a type (text, executable, directory — signalled by an extension or a magic number), a location (where its blocks are), a size, protection information (who may read, write, execute), and time stamps (created, modified, accessed). That metadata, not the data, is what a directory listing shows.

The operations are the system calls we met in Chapter 1: create, open, read, write, seek (reposition the file pointer), truncate, close, delete. open is the key one. It searches the directory, checks permissions once, and returns a small integer file descriptor pointing into the kernel’s open-file table, so later reads do not repeat the lookup. The kernel keeps two tables: a per-process table of descriptors and a system-wide table with the current file offset and a reference count. That split is why a parent and its forked child can share one file offset.

Programs access a file in one of two ways. Sequential access reads or writes records in order, like a tape — the common case. Direct (random) access jumps to any block by number — essential for databases. An indexed method builds an index so a record can be found by key, then read directly.

questions.prompt: What does open() return and why?

choices.text: The file’s contents.
The disk address of the file.
A small file descriptor referring to an entry in the kernel’s open-file table, so later reads and writes skip the directory lookup and permission check.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Contents are obtained by read().

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The descriptor is an index into a table; the disk address stays inside the kernel.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Opening once and then using the descriptor is far cheaper than naming the file in every call.

questions.prompt: Why can a forked child share the file offset with its parent?

choices.text: Because the child is a thread.
They share the same entry in the system-wide open-file table, which holds the offset.
Because files have no offset.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A forked child is a process.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only the per-process descriptor table is duplicated by fork.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Every open file has a current offset.

sections.title: Directories: structure and naming
sections.body:
A directory is itself a file whose contents map names to files. The structures have evolved. A single-level directory (one list for everyone) breaks at once on name clashes. A two-level directory gives each user a private list. A tree-structured directory lets users make subdirectories, giving every file a unique absolute path from the root (/home/ram/notes.txt) and allowing relative paths from the current directory (../notes.txt). An acyclic-graph directory allows a file or directory to appear under two names — sharing — through a link. A fully general graph allows cycles, which makes traversal and deletion dangerous and is generally avoided.

On Unix-style systems the name points to an inode: a small record holding the attributes and the locations of the data blocks. The name is only an entry in a directory, which is why two names can reach one inode — a hard link, with a reference count in the inode; the data is freed only when the count reaches zero. A symbolic (soft) link is instead a small file containing a path; it can cross file systems and may dangle if its target is deleted. Path lookup walks one component at a time: read the root directory, find the inode of home, read it, find ram, and so on — one or two disk accesses per component unless cached.

questions.prompt: What does deleting one of two hard links to a file do?

choices.text: Deletes the data immediately.
Turns the other link into a dangling pointer.
Removes one directory entry; the data stays until the link count reaches zero.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The other name still needs it.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is a symbolic link; hard links are equal peers.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The inode counts its names; only at zero are blocks freed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about symbolic links is true?

choices.text: They increase the inode’s reference count.
They are the same as hard links.
They store a path and can point to a directory on another file system or become dangling.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Only hard links do.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: They are a different mechanism.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A hard link cannot cross file systems because inode numbers are local to one.

figures.caption: Figure 6.2.1 — from a path to data
figures.note: Path lookup walks directories until it reaches the inode.

problems.prompt: A file has link count 3. One name is removed with rm. What is the link count, and is the data still accessible?
problems.answer: The link count becomes 2 and the data is still accessible through the two remaining names; the blocks are freed only when the count reaches 0 (and no process has the file open).

sections.title: Implementing a file system
sections.body:
A disk is carved into blocks (typically 4 KB), and the file system lays its structures on them. A typical Unix-style layout has: a boot block (to start the OS), a superblock (size, block count, free counts, where the other tables are), a free-space map, an inode table (the array of file records), and the data blocks. To protect against damage the superblock is replicated. In memory the kernel keeps the open-file tables, a mount table and caches of directory and inode data so that most operations avoid the disk.

Mounting attaches a file system to a point in the tree: the kernel reads its superblock, checks it, and records the mount point so lookups cross into the new tree. A virtual file system (VFS) layer makes this uniform: it defines a common interface (lookup, read, write) and each concrete file system — ext4, NTFS, FAT, NFS — plugs in its own implementation, so read() looks identical whether the file lives on a local SSD or a network server.

A concurrent-access note: when several processes use one file, the OS offers locks (shared for readers, exclusive for writers), and a consistency semantics: Unix lets a write be visible at once to others who have the file open; the Andrew file system makes changes visible only when the file is closed.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the virtual file system (VFS) layer?

choices.text: To give all file systems one common interface so the same system calls work on any of them.
To make files virtual so they use no disk space.
To compress files automatically.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each concrete file system supplies its own implementation behind the interface.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Files still occupy storage; “virtual” refers to the interface.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: VFS is about abstraction, not compression.

sections.title: Allocating disk blocks to files
sections.body:
How should a file’s blocks be placed? Contiguous allocation keeps the blocks side by side: sequential and random access are fast (one seek, then streaming), and a file is described by just a start block and a length. Its weaknesses are external fragmentation and the difficulty of growing a file; it persists in read-only media (CD-ROMs) and as extents (a start and length for each contiguous run) in modern file systems. Linked allocation chains the blocks: each block holds a pointer to the next. There is no fragmentation and files grow freely, but random access means following the chain — slow — and one lost pointer loses the rest of the file. The FAT (file allocation table) variant keeps all the pointers in one table at the start of the disk, cached in memory, which makes random access cheap and is why FAT survives on USB sticks.

Indexed allocation gives each file an index block (an array of block numbers); block k of the file is entry k. Random access is a single lookup and there is no external fragmentation. For large files the index must itself grow, so Unix inodes combine schemes: a number of direct pointers (small files need no more), then a single-indirect pointer to a block of pointers, a double-indirect pointer to a block of such blocks, and a triple-indirect level. Small files, the common case, are therefore reached with no extra I/O while very large files are still supported.

worked.why: Block size 4 KB, pointer size 4 bytes, so one block holds how many pointers?
An inode has 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect, one double-indirect and one triple-indirect pointer. Capacity from each level:
worked.math: 12\times4\text{ KB}=48\text{ KB},\ 1024\times4\text{ KB}=4\text{ MB},\ 1024^2\times4\text{ KB}=4\text{ GB},\ 1024^3\times4\text{ KB}=4\text{ TB}

worked.why: Maximum file size is the sum — dominated by the triple-indirect level.

questions.prompt: Which allocation method is best for random access?

choices.text: Linked.
None can do random access.
Indexed (or contiguous).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Random access means walking the chain.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Indexed can.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Block k is found by one index lookup; linked allocation must follow k pointers.

questions.prompt: Why does the Unix inode use direct pointers for the first blocks?

choices.text: Because direct pointers hold more data.
To prevent fragmentation.
Most files are small, so they are reached without any indirect block, saving disk accesses.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A pointer holds an address, not data.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Pointer type does not affect fragmentation.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Larger files pay for indirection only when they need it.

questions.prompt: What makes FAT better than plain linked allocation for random access?

choices.text: FAT stores files contiguously.
All the chain pointers sit in one table that can be cached in memory, so following the chain needs no disk reads.
FAT uses indexed allocation.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: FAT is a linked scheme.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The chain is the same but the pointers are gathered, not scattered inside data blocks.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: FAT is a table-based linked scheme.

problems.prompt: A file system has 8 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers; each inode has 10 direct pointers and one single-indirect pointer. What is the largest file it can hold?
problems.answer: Pointers per block = 8192 / 4 = 2048. Direct: 10 × 8 KB = 80 KB. Single indirect: 2048 × 8 KB = 16,384 KB = 16 MB. Total = 16,464 KB (≈ 16.08 MB).

problems.prompt: A disk has 2²⁸ blocks and a FAT entry is 4 bytes. How big is the FAT?
problems.answer: 2²⁸ × 4 B = 2³⁰ B = 1 GB — which is why FAT is impractical on very large disks (and the table must be cached).

sections.title: Free-space management
sections.body: The file system must know which blocks are free. A bit map (bit vector) has one bit per block — 1 free, 0 allocated; it is compact and makes finding a run of contiguous free blocks easy, but a large disk has a large bitmap. A linked list of free blocks needs no extra space but is slow to traverse. Grouping stores the addresses of n free blocks in the first free block, the last of which points to the next group. Counting stores (first free block, number of contiguous free blocks) pairs — good when free blocks come in runs. Modern file systems add space maps and delayed allocation (decide the layout at flush time, so many writes form one contiguous extent).

worked.why: A 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks. How many blocks?
A bit map needs one bit per block.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of a bit map for free-space management?

choices.text: It makes finding contiguous free blocks easy and uses one bit per block.
It needs no memory.
It records which file owns a block.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Scanning words of bits finds runs quickly.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: A big disk needs a big bit map.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It records only free/allocated.

problems.prompt: How large is a free-space bitmap for a 500 GB disk with 4 KB blocks?

sections.title: Performance and reliability: caching, journaling
sections.body:
Disks are slow, so file systems cache aggressively: the buffer cache keeps recently used blocks, read-ahead fetches the next blocks of a sequential file, and delayed write holds modified blocks in memory for seconds before flushing. The price is danger: a crash with dirty blocks in memory loses data and can leave the on-disk structures inconsistent — for example a new file’s directory entry is written but its inode is not. After such a crash the traditional repair tool (fsck) scans the whole disk and takes minutes to hours.

A journaling file system (ext3/4, NTFS, XFS) avoids that. Before changing the real structures it writes a short description of the intended change — a transaction — to a sequential log and commits it; only then does it apply the change in place. After a crash the log is replayed: committed transactions are redone, incomplete ones discarded, and the file system is consistent in seconds. Log-structured file systems go further and make the log the file system. Copy-on-write designs (ZFS, Btrfs) never overwrite a live block, so the old consistent tree remains valid until the new one is atomically published. Backups and snapshots complete the picture.

questions.prompt: What does a journaling file system do to recover quickly after a crash?

choices.text: It stores every file twice.
It replays or discards transactions recorded in the log instead of scanning the entire disk.
It never caches writes.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is mirroring, not journaling.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Metadata changes are written to the log first, so the log tells what was in progress.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It still caches; the log makes recovery safe.

sections.title: Protection: who may do what
sections.body:
Protection controls the access of programs, processes and users to resources defined by the system. The guiding rule is the principle of least privilege: give each subject exactly the access it needs and no more. The model is the access matrix: rows are domains (users or processes), columns are objects (files, devices), and each cell lists the rights (read, write, execute, own). The matrix is almost empty, so it is stored in slices. Cut by column, you get an access-control list (ACL) kept with each object: who may touch me. Cut by row, you get a capability list kept with each subject: what I may touch, a token the subject presents.

Classic Unix gives every file an owner, a group and three triples of permission bits — user, group, other — each with read (r = 4), write (w = 2) and execute (x = 1). The mode 750 means owner rwx, group r-x, others none. For a directory, “execute” means the right to traverse (look names up), and “read” the right to list. Special bits add setuid (run with the owner’s rights — how passwd can edit a protected file) and the sticky bit on shared directories like /tmp so users can delete only their own files. Many systems add richer ACLs, roles (role-based access control) and mandatory policies (SELinux) the user cannot override.

worked.why: Convert the mode rwxr-x--- to octal.
The octal mode is 750; the command is chmod 750 file.

questions.prompt: An access-control list is attached to…

choices.text: The user.
The CPU.
The object (file/resource): it lists who may do what.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is a capability.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Hardware only enforces privilege levels.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A capability list is attached to the subject instead.

questions.prompt: What does the principle of least privilege say?

choices.text: Every user should be an administrator.
Files should have no permissions.
Each subject should have only the access rights it needs to do its job.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The opposite of the principle.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Permissions are how least privilege is enforced.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A compromised or buggy program then does limited damage.

questions.prompt: Why does the passwd program need the setuid bit?

choices.text: To make it run faster.
To hide it from other users.
It must modify a password file the ordinary user cannot write, so it runs with the file owner’s (root’s) rights during execution.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Speed is unrelated.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: setuid is not about hiding.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is a controlled way to grant a specific, limited privilege.

figures.note: Three triples — user, group, other — each three bits r=4, w=2, x=1.

problems.prompt: Write the octal mode and the symbolic form for: owner read+write, group read, others none.
A directory has mode 700 and belongs to Ram. Can another user, Sita, list it, or read a file inside it with a known name?
problems.answer: No to both. Sita falls in “other” with no permissions, and she lacks execute (traverse) on the directory, so she cannot even look up the name of a file inside.

sections.title: Security: threats and defences
sections.body:
Protection assumes the system works as designed; security defends it against deliberate attack. The classic threats are malware (viruses attach to programs, worms spread by themselves over the network, trojans pretend to be useful, ransomware encrypts your files), buffer-overflow attacks (a program copies input into a fixed-size buffer without a length check, overwriting a neighbouring return address so the attacker’s code runs), denial of service (flood a service until it cannot answer), privilege escalation, eavesdropping and spoofing — and people, via phishing and weak passwords.

The defences are layered. Authentication proves who you are: something you know (a password, stored only as a salted hash), something you have (a phone or key), something you are (a fingerprint) — combined as multi-factor. Cryptography protects data: symmetric ciphers (AES) for bulk data, public-key ciphers (RSA, elliptic curves) for exchanging keys and signing, hashes (SHA-256) for integrity. The OS contributes memory protection, non-executable stacks and address-space layout randomisation against overflows, sandboxing to confine untrusted programs, secure boot to verify each boot stage’s signature, firewalls and intrusion detection, audit logs and prompt patching. Security is never finished; it is the art of making an attack cost more than it is worth.

questions.prompt: How does a stack buffer overflow let an attacker run code?

choices.text: It makes the disk fill up.
Excess input overwrites the saved return address next to the buffer so that, when the function returns, execution jumps to the attacker’s code.
It guesses the user’s password.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Overflow here is about memory bounds, not disk space.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Bounds checking, non-executable stacks and ASLR all defend against it.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It is a memory-corruption attack, not a password attack.

questions.prompt: Why are passwords stored as salted hashes?

choices.text: To make login faster.
To allow the admin to read passwords.
A hash cannot be reversed, and a unique salt per user defeats precomputed tables so identical passwords differ.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Hashing is deliberately slow.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The point is that nobody can read them.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A stolen password file then does not reveal the passwords directly.

figures.caption: Figure 6.8.1 — login then access
figures.note: Authentication first, then a check on every access.

problems.prompt: Why does two-factor authentication make a stolen password far less useful?
problems.answer: The attacker also needs a second, independent factor — a code from the user’s phone or hardware key — which a password leak does not reveal. The two factors fail independently, so the chance both are compromised is much smaller.

sections.title: Virtual machines and containers
sections.body:
A hypervisor (virtual machine monitor) lets several operating systems — guests — share one set of hardware, each believing it owns a whole computer. Type 1 hypervisors run directly on the hardware (Xen, VMware ESXi, KVM) and are the base of the cloud; Type 2 hypervisors run as an application on a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) and suit desktops. The trick is trapping: the guest kernel runs in user mode, so when it executes a privileged instruction the hardware traps to the hypervisor, which emulates the effect on the guest’s virtual device. Modern CPUs add hardware support (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) that makes this fast; memory is virtualised with nested page tables; I/O devices are emulated or passed through. Benefits: server consolidation, isolation, snapshots, live migration of a running VM between hosts.

A container (Docker, LXC) takes a lighter route and virtualises the operating system instead of the hardware: containers share one host kernel, but Linux namespaces give each its own view of processes, network, mounts and users, and cgroups limit its CPU, memory and I/O. There is no guest kernel to boot, so a container starts in milliseconds and uses little memory; the trade-off is weaker isolation (a kernel bug affects all) and the need for guests to use the same kernel. Orchestrators such as Kubernetes schedule thousands of containers across many machines.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start faster than a VM?

choices.text: Containers run on special hardware.
Containers are not isolated at all.
It has no guest kernel to boot — it shares the host’s.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: They run on ordinary hardware.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: They are isolated by namespaces and cgroups, though less strongly than VMs.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is just isolated processes.

questions.prompt: How does a Type 1 hypervisor stop a guest kernel from taking control of the hardware?

choices.text: It rewrites the guest’s source code.
It gives each guest its own physical CPU.
The guest runs unprivileged, so privileged instructions trap to the hypervisor, which emulates them on virtual devices.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The hypervisor works with unmodified binaries.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: CPUs are shared and scheduled.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Hardware virtualisation extensions make the trapping efficient.

figures.note: A VM carries a whole OS; a container shares the host kernel.

problems.prompt: Give one advantage and one risk of containers over virtual machines.
problems.answer: Advantage: start in milliseconds and use far less memory because they share the kernel. Risk: a kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host, and containers cannot run a different OS kernel.

sections.title: Contemporary systems
sections.body:
Linux is a monolithic, modular kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991, licensed under the GPL, with processes and threads scheduled by CFS, demand-paged virtual memory, a VFS with ext4 as the usual file system, and a huge driver collection; it runs everything from phones to supercomputers. Windows NT (the line from Windows NT to Windows 11) is a hybrid kernel with an object-oriented design, NTFS, a registry of configuration, and strong backward compatibility. macOS and iOS use XNU, a Mach–BSD hybrid with a proprietary user interface layer. Android runs a Linux kernel with a managed runtime (ART) above it and apps in sandboxes with a permission model. Embedded and real-time systems favour tiny kernels (FreeRTOS, Zephyr) with deadline-driven schedulers; robots add middleware such as ROS; smart-cards run minimal, tightly secured systems. Cloud and distributed systems add network file systems, replication and consensus.

The same five concerns — processes, memory, files, I/O and protection — recur in every one, with different priorities: throughput for servers, responsiveness for desktops, battery for phones, determinism for controllers. If you can explain each of the six chapters in this course for a Linux kernel, you can understand any other.

choices.text: Windows NT.
Linux.
A microkernel.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: No.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Android applications run on a managed runtime above a Linux kernel.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Linux is monolithic/modular.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling property matters most in a real-time embedded kernel?

choices.text: Maximum average throughput.
Predictable, bounded response so deadlines are met.
A graphical user interface.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A fast average can still miss a deadline.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Average throughput is secondary to guaranteed worst-case timing.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Many RTOSes have none.

problems.prompt: A 4 KB-block file system uses 12 direct and 1 single-indirect pointer (4-byte pointers). What is the largest file?
problems.answer: An indirect block holds 4096/4 = 1024 pointers. Total = (12 + 1024) × 4 KB = 4144 KB.

problems.prompt: Give one advantage and one risk of containers over VMs.
problems.answer: Advantage: start in milliseconds and use far less memory because they share the kernel. Risk: a kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host.

problems.prompt: Compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation on: random access, external fragmentation, file growth.
problems.answer: Contiguous: fast random access; external fragmentation; growth is hard. Linked: slow random access (follow the chain); no external fragmentation; growth easy. Indexed: fast random access; no external fragmentation; growth easy, up to the index size (extended with indirect blocks).

problems.prompt: Explain why a journaling file system can recover in seconds while fsck may take hours.
problems.answer: The journal records exactly which metadata updates were in progress, so recovery replays or discards only those transactions. fsck has no such record and must scan every inode, directory and the free map to find inconsistencies.

sections.title: Course summary
sections.body:
• The OS is an extended machine and resource manager, entered only through system calls and interrupts.
  • Processes and threads share the CPU by a scheduling policy; synchronisation tools prevent races; deadlock needs four conditions.
  • Paging with a TLB gives each process a private virtual address space; replacement and the working set govern performance.
  • I/O uses DMA and layered drivers; disks are scheduled to cut seeks; RAID adds speed and redundancy.
  • Files are named bytes; inodes, allocation and free-space maps organise the disk; journaling gives crash safety.
  • Protection (ACLs, capabilities, least privilege) and security (authentication, cryptography, isolation) defend the system; virtualisation and containers share one machine among many.
